title: Vortex
summary: Self-hosted media streaming on Android, Android TV and Windows - five real remote providers (Drive, SMB, SFTP, FTP, WebDAV), TMDB enrichment, offline downloads, Google Cast and a YouTube-powered music library.
description: Vortex is a client-side, self-hosted media streaming app with no backend and no subscription: it streams from sources you already own. It aggregates personal libraries from Google Drive, SMB, SFTP, FTP/FTPS and WebDAV behind one provider interface, discovers LAN servers over NSD/mDNS to pre-fill connection forms, and enriches everything with TMDB metadata cached locally. Playback is Media3/ExoPlayer with an FFmpeg software-decoder fallback on phones and TV, and an in-app mpv player on Windows. It adds per-profile state (favourites, watchlist, resume, subtitle and audio memory, kids profiles), picture-in-picture, Google Cast with its own LAN proxy, OpenSubtitles search, intro skip, a WorkManager download queue with quota cleanup, and a YouTube-powered music library with real offline downloads. Secrets live in an Android Keystore-backed encrypted store, never in the database.

title: CataAI
summary: A generative language model written from first principles - character-level tokenization and an autoregressive data pipeline today, then scaled dot-product attention, a Transformer block and a full training stack.
description: LLM from Scratch builds a language model without leaning on high-level model libraries, so every step is one I can explain and defend. The corpus is read once and tokenized into a vocabulary of unique symbols with bijective string-to-integer and integer-to-string maps; encode and decode are verified to round-trip. That vocabulary becomes a single long tensor, split into a train and a validation set so overfitting stays visible, and a batch sampler hands the model fixed-length context windows paired with their targets shifted one token ahead - the same next-token objective the whole system runs on. Everything after that is still being built: a small attention-free baseline to prove the pipeline end to end, then multi-head self-attention with a causal mask, a residual Transformer block, and a training and inference stack with warmup, cosine decay and top-k sampling.
features: Character-level tokenizer over the raw corpus - sorted unique symbols with bijective string-to-integer and integer-to-string maps
encode() and decode() verified to round-trip, so tokens can be mapped back to exactly the text they came from
Encoded corpus flattened into one long integer tensor, ready to be indexed into training windows
Train / validation split over the token stream, so generalization is measured rather than assumed
Batch sampler that hands out fixed-length context windows as input and target pairs, with targets shifted one token ahead
partialFeatures: Runs on CPU for now; the discrete GPU is currently disabled, so the CUDA path is installed but not exercised
plannedFeatures: A small attention-free baseline model to prove the training and sampling loop end to end
Multi-head scaled dot-product attention with a causal mask
A residual Transformer block with layer normalization
Training stack - warmup, cosine learning-rate decay and periodic validation
Inference sampling with temperature and top-k filtering
architecture: A single Python pipeline with clean seams between stages, each one consuming the output of the stage before it. The tokenizer turns raw text into an integer vocabulary and owns the two mapping directions. The data layer reads the corpus once, flattens the encoded tokens into one long tensor, splits it into train and validation, and hands out fixed-length windows whose targets are shifted a single token ahead. That shift is the whole point: every position in a window is a supervised next-token example, so a window of length T trains T predictions at once. The model side climbs from an attention-free baseline up to multi-head self-attention and a residual Transformer block, and the training loop wraps it with warmup, cosine decay and validation. Keeping the seams explicit means each stage can be swapped - character-level tokens for a subword vocabulary, the baseline for a Transformer - without touching the rest.
architectureDiagram:
Raw text corpus (input.txt)
        ↓
[ Tokenizer ]  unique symbols → stoi / itos maps
        ↓       encode(text) ↔ decode(tokens), round-trip verified
  Integer token stream
        ↓
[ Data layer ]  one long tensor → train / val split
        ↓       fixed-length windows, targets shifted +1 token
  (input, target) batches
        ↓
[ Model ]  baseline → self-attention → Transformer block
        ↓
[ Training loop ]  warmup + cosine decay + validation
        ↓
[ Inference ]  temperature + top-k sampling
limitations: Trains on CPU only for now - the discrete GPU is disabled, so the CUDA path is installed but unexercised
Character-level tokens give a tiny vocabulary but very long sequences, which costs compute per useful token
The corpus is a single local file, so the model only ever learns the distribution of that one text
No baseline loss has been recorded yet, so there is nothing to compare the Transformer against
futureWork: Swap character-level tokens for a subword (BPE) vocabulary to cut sequence length
Re-enable the discrete GPU and exercise the CUDA training path
Log training and validation loss across steps so progress and overfitting are visible
Move the corpus loading to a streaming reader so larger texts do not need to fit in memory
Sample and save generated text at checkpoints to eyeball quality over training

title: Cheltuieli
summary: A PyQt6 desktop expense tracker that scans IMAP inboxes for invoices, extracts amounts with OCR and PDF parsing, and exports everything to formatted Excel.

Scanning runs in background threads so the UI stays responsive.

title: Primarie (E-Services Portal)
summary: A municipal e-services portal - declarations, tax certificates and fine payments in one account - with scrypt auth, role-based dashboards, audit logging and SQLite storage.

title: Coral Tech · FTC team site
summary: Bilingual (EN/RO) site for an FTC robotics team - seasons, activities, members and sponsors, plus a two-game arcade, a page-flip photo album and a 10-module admin CMS behind passkeys and TOTP.
description: Coral Tech is the website of an FTC robotics team (#28260) - "fusing nature with technology". Twelve public routes cover seasons, activities, members, sponsors, outreach, recruitment and an interactive photo album; alongside them sit a two-game arcade (a procedural maze and an FTC logo-trivia game) and a 10-module admin CMS. Content is bilingual through hand-rolled locale files (275 keys in EN and RO, exact parity) with a per-entity field_en/field_ro convention. A local-LLM RAG assistant answers from the site's own content: chunks are embedded with Ollama or a local GGUF model and returned with citations plus allow-listed scroll actions. Admin auth is WebAuthn passkeys with TOTP 2FA and hashed single-use recovery codes.

title: Liceul Teoretic Ion Cantacuzino
summary: Full website for a Bucharest high school - 28 public routes over 16 SQLite tables, a 2,700-line timetable PDF parser, and an admin panel behind TOTP two-factor auth.
description: A complete school website built on Next.js and SQLite (better-sqlite3, WAL). It publishes news, classes, teachers, documents, results, gallery, a school magazine, case-study projects, FAQs, e-learning and timetables across 28 public routes. The distinguishing piece is a ~2,700-line timetable PDF parser that extracts a class schedule, associates teachers and resolves shift conflicts automatically, with class metadata (grade, profile, specialisation, head teacher, room) inferred from the parsed rows. Content is managed through an admin panel protected by JWT sessions, bcrypt hashing, TOTP two-factor authentication and CSRF double-submit tokens, with JSONL audit logging, progressive lockout and rate limiting. Uploaded files are validated by binary magic bytes. The public deployment is a static export; the admin panel, timetable parser, uploads and contact inbox require a Node server.
features: 28 public routes: news, classes, teachers, documents, results (3 routes), gallery, magazine, projects, FAQs, e-learning, timetables, educational offer and contact

Security headers - CSP, HSTS in production, X-Frame-Options DENY, nosniff, referrer and permissions policies
Image-optimizer SSRF allowlist in proxy.ts, and path-traversal-proof PDF resolution
GDPR privacy policy, terms of use, FAQ with a non-empty fallback, opening hours and a sticky mobile contact bar
No third-party analytics, an AI-crawler-readable llms.txt, and reduced-motion aware animated reveals
architecture: proxy.ts (the renamed middleware) guards every /admin and /api/admin request with a verified JWT, enforcing CSRF on mutations and applying an image-optimizer SSRF allowlist. Requests pass through a security tier - session verification, CSRF comparison, rate limiting, lockout and audit logging - into app/api/admin/* route handlers, which read and write through a content-store over a SQLite mapping layer down to better-sqlite3 in WAL mode. The timetable PDF parser runs server-side against uploaded documents and returns rows, warnings and diagnostics. The production build is a static export to GitHub Pages with the admin and API trees stripped, so the write paths only exist under next dev or a self-hosted Node runtime.

    ↓
content-store.ts → sqlite-content.ts (11 entities)
    ↓
better-sqlite3 (WAL) → data/db.sqlite

Break up the timetable parser and the content mapper, and add a real test framework

title: YOLO Trainer
summary: A PySide6 desktop app for training, fine-tuning and testing YOLO models (v8/11/26) with live logs, metric charts, GPU checks and a packaged Windows installer.
description: YOLO Trainer is a desktop GUI around Ultralytics training. It splits the workflow into Train, Fine-tune and Test tabs, runs training in a QThread so the UI stays live, plots metrics with pyqtgraph, validates datasets and presets, and supports inference on images, videos or folders. It can be packaged as a Windows installer (PyInstaller + Inno Setup) and supports WebSocket-based remote inference.
features: Train / fine-tune / test tabs with preset configurations
Background training via QThread with live logs and progress
Metric plotting (pyqtgraph / matplotlib)
Inference testing on images, video and folders
Dataset validation before training
GPU detection and configuration
Dark theme UI
Windows installer packaging (PyInstaller spec + Inno Setup script)
WebSocket-based remote inference
architecture: Training runs in a QThread worker (workers/training_worker.py) that reports logs and metrics to the UI; services wrap Ultralytics, GPU discovery, dataset validation and preset loading; widgets render logs and metric plots; inference workers handle test-time detection.
architectureDiagram:
PySide6 UI (tabs: train · finetune · test)
    ↓  QThread workers
Ultralytics YOLO (train / finetune / predict)
    ├─ dataset_service (validation)
    ├─ gpu_service (CUDA)
    └─ preset_service (YAML presets)
limitations: Training requires the PyTorch/CUDA toolchain
WebSocket inference needs a running receiver

title: Jarvis · OS Helper
summary: A local-first AI operating assistant: a 9B planner, a 26M executor, 56 tools, and an offline keyword router so everything keeps working without a model server.
description: Jarvis is a local-first, extensible AI assistant built on the @earendil-works/pi framework. It uses a three-layer architecture - Ornith (9B) plans but never calls tools, Needle (26M) picks tool + args but never chats, and the runtime validates, checks permissions, executes and logs. There are 56 tools across filesystem, shell, Windows, Excel, browser, memory, media, system, archive, document, image, AI, automation and dev groups. A correction layer routes intents offline - fixing typos, Unix aliases and known failure modes - so all tools stay reachable even when no model is running. The media manager syncs a Google Drive / local library and talks to qBittorrent and rclone.
features: Three-layer agent architecture: planner (9B) → executor (26M) → runtime
56 tools in 14 groups with a permissions system (safe/ask)
Offline correction-layer router: typo tolerance, Unix aliases, multilingual hints, legacy failure fixes
Media manager: filelist (SQLite-cached library), drive (rclone), torrent (qBittorrent WebUI)
Persistence: media index and memory stores in SQLite
GPU Docker workspace (CUDA Jupyter) via docker-compose
Test suite (Jest) covering executor, permissions, media and tools
Documentation for installation, extensions, workflows and model optimization
architecture: Queries flow User → Ornith (planner) → Needle (executor) → Runtime → Tools. The runtime validates and gates tool calls by permission; when Needle is unavailable, correction.ts routes intents via a prioritized keyword scorer so the same tools stay reachable offline. Media tooling caches library state in media_index.db and integrates rclone + qBittorrent.
architectureDiagram:
User
  ↓
Ornith (planner, 9B) - plans, never calls tools
  ↓
Needle (executor, 26M) - picks tool + args
  ↓
Runtime (validate · permissions · execute · log)
  ↓
56 tools - filesystem · shell · windows · excel · browser · media · AI …

correction.ts routes intents offline when Needle is down
limitations: Relies on the @earendil-works/pi framework as the host platform
Requires bundled binaries (ffmpeg, rclone) and optional qBittorrent for media tools

title: Siteauto
summary: A car-parts shop with AI detection: upload a photo and a custom YOLOv8 model identifies the part and matches products - plus cart, checkout, appointments and a dashboard.
description: Siteauto is a Next.js storefront for car parts with a computer-vision twist: the detect page accepts a photo, runs a custom-trained YOLOv8 model (there are variants trained with and without side mirrors), draws the detected part on a canvas and filters matching products. The store itself has products, a cart (Redis-backed), checkout, JWT auth, service appointments, a dashboard for cars and messages, 3D product models and a floating chat widget. The detection runs through a Python helper spawned by the Next.js API route.
features: Photo upload with canvas preview and YOLOv8 part detection (custom model, .15 confidence floor)
Detection results matched against store products
Shop with product pages and 3D product models
Cart + checkout flow
Register/login with JWT sessions
Service appointments and dashboard (appointments, cars, messages)
Floating chat widget
Docker deployment with Python/OpenCV system deps
architecture: app/api/detect/route.js spawns utils/detect.py (Ultralytics YOLO + OpenCV) as a child process, parses its JSON output, and matches classes to products. The store layer uses Redis via lib/redis.js for cart state, and JWT middleware guards the dashboard/checkout routes. Custom .pt models live in model/.
architectureDiagram:
Browser (upload photo)
    ↓
Next.js /api/detect → python utils/detect.py (YOLOv8)
    ↓  JSON detections
product matching → shop / cart (Redis) / checkout (JWT)
limitations: Requires Redis running locally for cart functionality
Detection runs a Python subprocess per request - fine for a demo, not for scale
Model files (.pt) are large binaries kept in the repo

title: AI Interface
summary: A small Flask app that classifies uploaded images with locally loaded TensorFlow models, plus a helper that indexes a folder into a dataset manifest.
description: AI Interface is a compact experiment: a Flask web app that loads Keras models registered in models.json, accepts an image upload, runs inference with the selected model and returns the predicted class. A companion tkinter script walks a directory of images and writes top_level_folders.json - a small helper for assembling image datasets for training.
features: Image upload and classification against a user-selected model
Model registry in models.json mapping keys to .h5 weights and label files
GET /models endpoint listing available models
Folder-indexing helper that writes top_level_folders.json from a directory
architecture: A single Flask process serves the HTML frontend from templates/, accepts uploads into uploads/, and runs tf.keras inference per request. Models are loaded from .h5 files on disk per the models.json registry.
limitations: One-shot inference only - no batching, no GPU path, no error fallback beyond the Flask defaults
Models must be placed manually under models/

title: LLM Finetuner
summary: A Flask web interface for fine-tuning LLMs with Unsloth - LoRA parameters, live GPU monitoring, custom chat templates and training resume.
description: LLM Finetuner puts Unsloth-based LoRA fine-tuning behind a web UI. It ships with model presets (Llama 3.2 1B, Mistral 7B 4-bit), configurable LoRA/training parameters, GPU/CPU/system metrics streamed from the backend, custom chat templates, live training logs and a resume flow. Heavy imports (Unsloth, TRL, Transformers) load lazily so the UI stays responsive, and everything runs locally.
features: Fine-tune any Unsloth-compatible model from a web form
Model presets in config/models.json (e.g. Llama 3.2 1B Instruct, Mistral 7B v0.3, 4-bit variants)
Configurable LoRA + training parameters (rank, alpha, dropout, batch, grad accumulation, warmup, max steps, learning rate)
Custom chat template support with defaults in config/default_template.json
Live GPU / CPU / system metrics (nvidia-smi, WMI/win32pdh on Windows, psutil)
Live training logs and status tracking
Training resume from a saved state (resume.html)
Lazy loading of heavy ML imports; uploads and cache directories managed by the app
Example training dataset included (data.json - car-diagnostics chat pairs)
architecture: Flask serves the web UI and defers to a lazily-imported finetunerLLM module that drives Unsloth's FastLanguageModel with TRL's SFTTrainer. Training runs on a background thread while a status object tracks progress and messages. Config lives in JSON files under config/ (models, default settings, templates).
architectureDiagram:
Browser (index · resume)
    ↓
Flask app.py
    ├─ finetunerLLM (Unsloth + SFTTrainer)
    ├─ utils/system_monitor (GPU/CPU metrics)
    └─ config/*.json (models · settings · templates)
limitations: Requires a CUDA GPU with enough VRAM and the CUDA toolchain (tested on 12.4)
Requires an Unsloth-compatible model
Training is local-only - no distributed or cloud training

title: NeuroShell
summary: A Claude Code-style terminal AI shell: slash commands, tab completion, instant model hot-swapping across Ollama/GGUF/Transformers/HF/OpenAI, and a sandboxed tool loop.
description: NeuroShell is an interactive terminal shell and autonomous tool-using AI agent. It brings a Claude Code-like command interface with a slash-command palette, real-time tab autocompletion, instant model swapping across five backends (Ollama, local GGUF, PyTorch Transformers, Hugging Face cloud, OpenAI-compatible endpoints), and a sandboxed tool-execution loop that restricts filesystem and terminal actions to the configured workspace. It includes a GPU device abstraction (CUDA with automatic CPU fallback), Hugging Face model downloads with cache management, dialogue memory, RAG command indexing, and optional voice input/output.
features: Interactive REPL with a slash-command palette (/help, /model, /gpu, /download, /clear, /tools, /mode, /history, /exit)
Real-time tab autocompletion for commands, models, Hugging Face repos and workspace paths
Instant model hot-swapping across Ollama, local GGUF, Transformers, HF Cloud and OpenAI-compatible endpoints
Autonomous tool-use loop with planning, intent classification, task state and reflection modules
Sandboxed execution: filesystem/terminal restricted to the workspace; dangerous commands blocked; Safe Mode asks before modifying
GPU device abstraction with /gpu diagnostics (device, name, VRAM) and CPU fallback
Hugging Face model downloading with cache management (HF_HOME isolated)
Dialogue history (JSONL) and execution memory
RAG command indexing and project-aware helpers (project detection, brain, summarizer)
Optional voice: STT/TTS with wake word and auto language detection
PyInstaller-friendly entry point with pip-subprocess support
architecture: A prompt_toolkit REPL (ui/cli.py) drives a turn loop (core/loop.py) that routes intents through a tool router to sandboxed executors. Models are managed by models/manager.py across five providers, with a GPU device layer (gpu/device.py) mapping tensors to cuda:0 or cpu. State (config, registry, history) lives under ~/.neuroshell/, with caches isolated there too.
architectureDiagram:
Terminal REPL (prompt_toolkit)
    ↓
core/loop (agent · planner · router)
    ↓
tools (terminal · filesystem · system · web) - sandboxed
    ↑
models/manager → ollama · GGUF · transformers · HF · OpenAI
limitations: Local model quality depends on the active backend/model
Requires Python 3.10+ and (for GPU) an NVIDIA GPU with the CUDA wheels
